title: Verbs in -er
topic: present tense of regular -er verbs; negation ne… pas
why: After être and avoir, this lesson opens the biggest family of French verbs, the regular -er verbs, and the negation ne… pas. You can now say your name, where you live, what you do and what you like, and spot the silent -ent that trips up English speakers.

One pattern for hundreds of verbs

Most French verbs end in -er in the infinitive: parler (to speak), habiter (to live), travailler (to work)… And good news: they are almost all regular. Take off -er and add the endings -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.

parler (to speak)habiter (to live)aimer (to like, to love)
je / j'je parlej'habitej'aime
tutu parlestu habitestu aimes
il, elle, onil parleelle habiteon aime
nousnous parlonsnous habitonsnous aimons
vousvous parlezvous habitezvous aimez
ils, ellesils parlentelles habitentils aiment

Four forms, one sound

Here is the surprise: parle, parles, parle and parlent are pronounced exactly the same, “parl”. Only parlons and parlez sound different. The -ent of ils parlent is completely silent: it never sounds like the “-ent” of “parent” or “went”. This is the classic mistake of English speakers reading aloud.

As with j'ai, je becomes j' before a vowel or a silent h: j'habite, j'aime, j'écoute, j'étudie. And the s of nous, vous, ils, elles is linked to a vowel with a “z” sound: nous‿habitons, vous‿aimez, ils‿arrivent.

Ils parlent anglais et elles habitent à Lyon.They speak English and they live in Lyon.

étudier keeps its i everywhere: j'étudie, nous étudions, ils étudient (the -ent is silent here too).

", "

Ne… pas: saying no

To make a sentence negative, French puts two words around the verb: ne before, pas after. Before a vowel or a silent h, ne becomes n'.

Je ne travaille pas le samedi.I don't work on Saturdays.
Elle n'habite pas à Lyon.She doesn't live in Lyon.
Nous ne sommes pas anglais.We aren't English.
Je n'aime pas le sport.I don't like sports.

No “do” in French

English needs “do” or “does” to make a negative or a question: “I don't work”, “Do you work?”. French has nothing of the kind: just the verb with ne… pas, or the verb with a rising voice.

EnglishFrench
I don't speak Spanish.Je ne parle pas espagnol.
Do you speak French?Tu parles français ?
Does she work here?Elle travaille ici ?

Never add a verb for “do” and never forget ne in writing. In relaxed speech, the French often drop it (je travaille pas): you'll hear it everywhere, but write the full form.

le samedi means “on Saturdays”, every Saturday. Take it as an expression for now: days of the week come in unit 2.

", "

One present, three Englishes

French has a single present tense. Je travaille can mean “I work”, “I'm working” or “I do work”: the context does the rest. Never try to translate “am working” word for word (“je suis travaille” does not exist).

Je travaille à la gare.I work at the station. / I'm working at the station.

Verbs without a preposition

Some verbs need a little word in English but not in French. These are false friends of structure:

  • écouter = to listen to: j'écoute la musique.
  • regarder = to look at, to watch: il regarde la télévision.
  • chercher = to look for: je cherche la gare.
  • rester = to stay, not “to rest”: je reste à Paris (I'm staying in Paris).

Likes and dislikes

With aimer and détester, French uses le, la, les for things in general, where English uses nothing: j'aime la musique (I like music), je déteste le sport. Same with languages you study: j'étudie le français, but je parle français, with no article after parler.

Your name

To give your name, say je m'appelle (literally “I call myself”): tu t'appelles, il s'appelle, elle s'appelle. Learn it as a fixed expression: verbs like this one are explained in unit 2.

Je m'appelle Julien, j'habite à Nantes et j'aime le cinéma.My name is Julien, I live in Nantes and I like movies.

dîner is both a verb (to have dinner) and a noun, le dîner: nous dînons à la maison.
